title: Builders' Site
strapline: Hard hats on — there's a wall to build, a wheelbarrow to push and a plan to follow.
intent: The site turns construction into a shared human project: builders work in teams, follow plans, fetch materials and solve problems together.
Lifting crates, pushing loaded wheelbarrows and hauling big blocks is proper whole-body work with a purpose.
Tools used properly — hammers, spanners, trowels, tape measures — build hand control and the satisfaction of doing a real job well.
Building talk is measuring talk: longer, taller, heavier, next to, on top, not enough bricks — maths with a hard hat on.
Plans, walls that fall down and materials that run out give children real problems worth persisting through.
Negotiating who drives the digger and who mixes the cement keeps cooperation under constant, happy strain.
implementation: Join the crew as a labourer, not the foreman: 'Where do you want these bricks, boss?' hands children the planning role.
Model site talk and measuring talk: 'this plank's too short', 'we need two more', 'is it level?', 'steady — that's heavy.'
Draw simple plans together before building, and return to them: 'the plan says the wall goes here — how many bricks tall?'
Provide honest weight: crates, guttering, planks and big blocks that genuinely take effort (and sometimes a friend) to move.
Add tape measures, spirit levels and clipboards, and treat measuring and 'site checks' as real jobs.
When the tower collapses, resist rescuing — 'what happened? What could we try instead?' is where the learning lives.
Watch real diggers and scaffolding on local walks, then feed what children noticed back into the site.
key_questions: What are you building — and what does the plan say to do first?
How many more bricks will you need to finish the wall?
That fell down! What could you try differently this time?
Which plank is longer? Will it reach across the gap?
This is too heavy for one builder — what shall we do?

impact.text: Children build with clear purpose — a wall, a garage, a tower for the crane — and tell you all about what it is and what happens next.
Children build to a plan — 'we're making a bridge' — and adapt it when the planks don't reach or the tower leans.
The crew sustains a shared site storyline, negotiating roles — digger driver, crane operator, foreman — narrating and directing the job aloud as it goes.
Children push, pull and carry genuinely heavy loads on purpose, and move around the site with control.
Children use tools with intent — tapping, twisting, smoothing, measuring — handling them safely and effectively.
Children use positional and comparative language constantly as they build: longer, heavier, on top, next to, not enough.
Children count bricks with one-to-one accuracy and lay them in repeating patterns, predicting what comes next in the row.
Children stick with a tricky build through collapses and re-tries — and announce 'I did it!' when the wall finally stands.

enhancements: Hard hats, high-vis vests and a site sign with the builders' names on it.
Real short lengths of guttering, drainpipe and planks for ramps and water runs.
A wheelbarrow and crates for genuinely heavy haulage.
Tape measures, spirit levels, clipboards and pencils for site surveys.
Sand and trowels for 'cement', with brushes for sweeping up after.
Laminated photo plans of simple structures to build from — then children draw their own.
A walk to watch real scaffolding, a cement mixer or a digger at work locally.

playing_exploring: Children throw their whole bodies into a grown-up world of hard hats and heavy loads they usually only watch through fences.
Every material asks a question — will it balance, will it reach, will it hold?
active_learning: Walls fall down here daily; the builders go again, adjusting their method — persistence with a hard hat on.
creating_thinking: Children plan, test, hit problems and change approach — the full engineering loop, run at nursery scale.
